questions.q: In what form does a Kafka broker store a record's key and value?

options.t: As JSON documents it can index and query
options.why: The broker doesn't parse records; it stores bytes.

options.t: As bytes; clients serialize and deserialize them
As Java objects, so only Java clients can read them
options.why: Any client can read the bytes; the format is agreed between producers and consumers.

options.t: As Avro, which the broker converts on write
options.why: Apache Kafka brokers do no format conversion.

questions.explain: Keys and values are bytes to the broker. The producer's serializer and the consumer's deserializer must agree on the format.

questions.q: A team wants to produce Avro records with the plain Apache Kafka Java client. Which serializer ships with Apache Kafka for this?

options.t: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.AvroSerializer
options.why: There is no such class in Apache Kafka.

options.t: StringSerializer with an Avro schema property
options.why: StringSerializer encodes strings; it has no schema support.

options.t: ByteArraySerializer, which validates Avro
options.why: ByteArraySerializer passes bytes through unchanged.

options.t: None; Avro serializers come with Schema Registry

questions.explain: Apache Kafka ships serializers for strings, numbers, bytes, UUIDs, lists and void, but none for Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema; those come with Confluent's Schema Registry.

questions.q: In `org.apache.kafka.common.serialization`, what is a `Serde<T>`?

options.t: A serializer and a deserializer for one type, wrapped together
A broker plugin that converts formats
options.why: Serdes are client-side; brokers don't convert formats.

options.t: A schema stored in the cluster metadata
options.why: Schemas are not stored in Kafka's metadata.

options.t: A serializer that only works in Kafka Connect
options.why: Serdes are used by Kafka Streams and any client code.

questions.explain: `Serde<T>` is the interface wrapping a serializer and a deserializer for a type; `Serdes` is a factory (`Serdes.String()`, `Serdes.Long()`, …).

questions.q: A consumer reads a topic where some records are JSON and some are plain text, and fails with a JSON decode error. What is the underlying problem?

options.t: The broker corrupted the plain-text records
options.why: Brokers store bytes as written.

options.t: The topic needs more partitions
options.why: Partition count has nothing to do with record format.

options.t: Schemaless JSON enforces nothing, so producers wrote mixed formats
JSON records must be compressed
options.why: Compression doesn't change the record format.

questions.explain: JSON with no schema carries field names in every record and enforces nothing; a topic mixing plain text and JSON is the classic failure. A schema and a registry make producers agree.

questions.q: In Schema Registry, what is the default compatibility type?

options.t: FORWARD
options.why: FORWARD is available but not the default.

options.t: FULL_TRANSITIVE
options.why: Available, but not the default.

options.t: NONE
options.why: NONE turns checks off and is not the default.

options.t: BACKWARD

questions.explain: The default compatibility is BACKWARD: consumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous one.

questions.q: A subject uses BACKWARD compatibility and a new schema version is registered. Which should be upgraded first?

options.t: The consumers
The producers
options.why: Producers go first under FORWARD compatibility.

options.t: Both at exactly the same moment
options.why: That's needed by no mode; FULL allows upgrading in any order.

options.t: The brokers
options.why: Brokers don't read schemas.

questions.explain: BACKWARD: upgrade consumers first, because the new schema can read old data. FORWARD: producers first. FULL: independently.

questions.q: An Avro schema gains a new field. For readers on the new schema to still read records written before the change, what must the field have?

options.t: A union type with null in second place
options.why: The rule is about a default value, not a particular union layout.

options.t: A default value
The same name as a removed field
options.why: Reusing names doesn't make old data readable.

options.t: A larger field number than every other field
options.why: Field numbers belong to Protobuf, not Avro.

questions.explain: In Avro schema resolution, a field the reader has but the writer didn't takes the reader's default; without a default it is an error. So an added field needs a default.

questions.q: A Protobuf message field number 4 is no longer used. What should the developer do with it?

options.t: Reuse 4 for the next new field to keep numbers compact
options.why: Reusing a field number breaks old data and readers.

options.t: Renumber the remaining fields to close the gap
options.why: A field number can't change once in use.

options.t: Mark 4 as reserved so it is never reused
Nothing; Protobuf identifies fields by name
options.why: On the wire, Protobuf identifies fields by number.

questions.explain: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire; a number can't change once in use, and deleted numbers should be reserved and never reused.

questions.q: What does a `*_TRANSITIVE` compatibility type (for example BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE) add?

options.t: It also checks the schema on the broker
options.why: Compatibility is checked by Schema Registry, not brokers.

options.t: It applies the rule to keys as well as values
options.why: Keys and values each have their own subject.

options.t: It disables checks for minor versions
options.why: It checks more, not less.

options.t: A check against every earlier version, not just the last

questions.explain: Transitive types check a new schema against all earlier versions in the subject, not just the latest one.

questions.q: With Schema Registry's default wire format, what comes before the encoded data in a record's value?

options.t: A magic byte 0, then a 4-byte schema ID
The full schema text as JSON
options.why: Sending the schema with every record is what the registry avoids.

options.t: The subject name and version number
options.why: The prefix is the schema ID, not the subject and version.

options.t: Nothing; the schema ID is a record header
options.why: In the default format the ID is in the payload prefix; a header option came later.

questions.explain: Byte 0 is a magic byte 0, bytes 1-4 the schema ID (big-endian), then (for Protobuf) a message index, then the data.

questions.q: A topic must carry several record types (OrderCreated, OrderShipped) with their own schemas. Which subject naming strategy is meant for this?

options.t: TopicNameStrategy, the default
options.why: It derives one subject from the topic, so one schema per topic.

options.t: TopicRecordNameStrategy
PartitionNameStrategy
options.why: No such strategy exists.

options.t: HeaderNameStrategy
options.why: No such strategy exists.

questions.explain: `TopicNameStrategy` (the default) derives the subject from the topic, so one schema per topic. `TopicRecordNameStrategy` derives it from the topic and the record type, for several record types in one topic.

questions.q: What can a Kafka record header hold?

options.t: Only one header per record
options.why: A record can have many headers, even with the same key.

options.t: Any Java object, serialized by the producer
options.why: Header values are byte arrays; you serialize them yourself.

options.t: A String key and a byte[] value
Only routing information read by the broker
options.why: Brokers don't route by headers; they are for applications.

questions.explain: A header is a `String` key with a `byte[]` value (which may be null), and multiple headers may share a key.

questions.q: A record carries two headers with key `trace`. What does `headers.lastHeader("trace")` return?

options.t: The first one added
options.why: lastHeader returns the last one.

options.t: An error, because keys must be unique
options.why: Multiple headers may have the same key.

options.t: Both values concatenated
options.why: It returns a single header.

options.t: The last one added

questions.explain: `lastHeader(key)` returns the very last header for the key; `headers(key)` returns all of them in the order they were added.

questions.q: Which TWO are good uses of record headers?

options.t: A correlation or trace ID that travels with the event
The partition number the broker should use
options.why: Partitions are chosen by the producer, not by headers.

options.t: Metadata such as the event type, without changing the value's format
The record's offset, set by the producer
options.why: Offsets are assigned by the broker.

options.t: A replacement for the key in compaction
options.why: Compaction works on keys, not headers.

questions.explain: Headers are optional key-value metadata on a record, read by applications; they carry things like trace IDs or event types without changing the key or value.

questions.q: How do you wait for the result of an Admin API call such as `createTopics` in a synchronous program?

options.t: Call get() on the KafkaFuture in its result
Call poll() on the Admin client
options.why: poll() is a consumer method.

options.t: Admin calls are always synchronous
options.why: Admin methods return futures; get() makes them synchronous.

options.t: Sleep until the topic appears in kafka-topics --list
options.why: The future already tells you when the call finished.

questions.explain: Admin methods return results holding `KafkaFuture`s; for synchronous behaviour, call `KafkaFuture.get()`.

questions.q: An application calls `admin.createPartitions` asking for 4 partitions on a topic that has 6. What happens?

options.t: The topic is shrunk to 4 partitions
options.why: Partitions can only be increased.

options.t: The two newest partitions are merged into the others
options.why: Kafka never merges partitions.

options.t: It fails with InvalidPartitionsException
It succeeds but takes effect after a broker restart
options.why: The request is rejected outright.

questions.explain: `createPartitions` only increases. A count less than or equal to the current one fails with `InvalidPartitionsException`; Kafka cannot reduce a topic's partitions.

questions.q: Which Admin API method changes one topic setting, such as `retention.ms`, without resetting the topic's other settings?

options.t: createTopics with the same name
options.why: That fails for an existing topic.

options.t: describeConfigs
options.why: That only reads configuration.

options.t: alterConsumerGroupOffsets
options.why: That changes a group's offsets, not topic configs.

options.t: incrementalAlterConfigs

questions.explain: `incrementalAlterConfigs` changes individual settings; `describeConfigs` reads them.

questions.q: A team must remove records before offset 10 000 in partition 0 of a topic with the delete cleanup policy, without deleting the topic. Which Admin API method does that?

options.t: deleteRecords
deleteTopics with a partition filter
options.why: deleteTopics deletes whole topics.

options.t: deleteConsumerGroupOffsets
options.why: That removes a group's committed offsets, not records.

options.t: incrementalAlterConfigs with retention.ms=0 on partition 0
options.why: Retention is per topic, not per partition.

questions.explain: `deleteRecords` deletes records whose offset is smaller than the given offset for a partition.

questions.q: Which TWO tasks can the Admin API do?

options.t: Create ACLs
Produce records to a topic
options.why: Producing is the producer's job.

options.t: Reset a consumer group's committed offsets
Change a broker's JVM heap size
options.why: JVM options are not Kafka configs the Admin API manages.

options.t: Read records from a topic
options.why: Reading is the consumer's job.

questions.explain: The Admin client manages and inspects topics, brokers, configurations and ACLs (`createAcls`), and consumer group offsets (`alterConsumerGroupOffsets`).

questions.q: Is the Admin client safe to share between threads?

options.t: No; create one per thread
options.why: Instances from Admin.create are guaranteed thread safe.

options.t: Only for read-only calls
options.why: The guarantee covers the instance as a whole.

options.t: Yes; Admin.create returns thread-safe instances
Only if every call uses get()
options.why: Thread safety doesn't depend on how results are awaited.

questions.explain: Instances returned by `Admin.create` are guaranteed to be thread safe.

questions.q: Order events must be processed in order for each order, and the latest state of each order must be easy to rebuild. Which key should the producer use?

options.t: A random UUID per event
options.why: Random keys spread one order's events over partitions, losing their order.

options.t: The event type
options.why: All orders' events of one type would share a partition, and one order's events would be split by type.

options.t: The order ID
No key, for the best balance
options.why: Without a key, one order's events can land in different partitions.

questions.explain: Events with the same key go to the same partition and are read in order; keying by order ID also lets a compacted topic keep the latest state per order.
